## Why this unit matters

- **Sensitivity:** which inputs move a chosen output?
- **Identifiability:** which parameters can the observation process distinguish?
- A narrow optimizer interval is not evidence that every biological parameter is learned.

::: {.notes}
This deck is a map of the detailed book chapter. Keep the distinction between
perturbing a model and learning from data visible throughout the presentation.
:::

## Baseline SIR model

Deterministic, continuous-time, continuous-state, population model:

$$
\dot S=-\beta cSI/N,\qquad
\dot I=\beta cSI/N-\gamma I,\qquad
\dot R=\gamma I.
$$

At the course baseline,
$N=1000$, $(S,I,R)=(990,10,0)$,
$(\beta,c,\gamma)=(0.05,10,0.25)$, and
$\mathcal R_0=\beta c/\gamma=2$.

The state sensitivity matrix is
$J_x(t)=\partial x(t)/\partial(\beta,c,\gamma)$.

::: {.notes}
The product beta times c is the transmission rate in this model. That
observation previews the structural identifiability result.
:::

## Local sensitivity: a derivative, not an uncertainty interval

For a small perturbation,

$$
\Delta z\approx\nabla_\theta z\,\Delta\theta.
$$

The following small solve uses `OrdinaryDiffEq` and centered perturbations to
plot the infectious-state derivative at the baseline.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-slide-ch10-local
#| fig-cap: "Centered local derivatives of infectious prevalence."
using CairoMakie
using OrdinaryDiffEq

course_root = normpath(joinpath(@__DIR__, "..", ".."))
include(joinpath(course_root, "src", "EpiModelingCourse.jl"))
using .EpiModelingCourse

const N10 = BASELINE_PARAMETERS.N
const u010 = [BASELINE_INITIAL_STATE.S, BASELINE_INITIAL_STATE.I,
    BASELINE_INITIAL_STATE.R]
function sir10!(du, u, p, t)
    β, c, γ = p
    incidence = β * c * u[1] * u[2] / N10
    du[1] = -incidence
    du[2] = incidence - γ * u[2]
    du[3] = γ * u[2]
end

times10 = collect(0.0:1.0:40.0)
p010 = [0.05, 10.0, 0.25]
base10 = Array(solve(ODEProblem(sir10!, u010, (0.0, 40.0), p010),
    Tsit5(); saveat = times10))
local10 = Matrix{Float64}(undef, length(times10), 3)
for j in 1:3
    δ = 1e-5 * p010[j]
    plus = copy(p010); plus[j] += δ
    minus = copy(p010); minus[j] -= δ
    up = Array(solve(ODEProblem(sir10!, u010, (0.0, 40.0), plus),
        Tsit5(); saveat = times10))[2, :]
    um = Array(solve(ODEProblem(sir10!, u010, (0.0, 40.0), minus),
        Tsit5(); saveat = times10))[2, :]
    local10[:, j] = (up .- um) ./ (2δ)
end
fig10 = Figure(size = (800, 430))
ax10 = Axis(fig10[1, 1], xlabel = "time", ylabel = "∂I/∂parameter")
for (j, label) in enumerate(["β", "c", "γ"])
    lines!(ax10, times10, local10[:, j], label = label)
end
axislegend(ax10)
fig10
```

::: {.notes}
The derivative is local to the baseline and depends on the chosen output,
time, and parameterization. A derivative is not a posterior distribution.
:::

## Global variation and the observation map

Global analysis varies a plausible parameter box and summarizes an output such
as peak infectious prevalence. `GlobalSensitivity.gsa` can replace the small
grid below with a Sobol design; the interpretation still depends on the bounds.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-slide-ch10-global
#| fig-cap: "One-at-a-time output ranges over a plausible parameter box."
function peak10(p)
    sol = solve(ODEProblem(sir10!, u010, (0.0, 40.0), p),
        Tsit5(); saveat = 1.0)
    maximum(Array(sol)[2, :])
end
boxes10 = [[0.02, 0.08], [5.0, 15.0], [0.15, 0.40]]
effects10 = [peak10([j == k ? boxes10[j][2] : p010[j] for j in 1:3]) -
    peak10([j == k ? boxes10[j][1] : p010[j] for j in 1:3]) for k in 1:3]
fig10g = Figure(size = (750, 400))
ax10g = Axis(fig10g[1, 1], xticks = (1:3, ["β", "c", "γ"]),
    ylabel = "change in peak I")
barplot!(ax10g, 1:3, effects10)
fig10g
```

Only incidence is observed:

$$
y(t)=\beta c\,S(t)I(t)/N.
$$

The transformation $(\beta,c)\mapsto(a\beta,c/a)$ leaves this map unchanged.
Thus $\beta$ and $c$ are structurally confounded; $\beta c$ can be learned.

::: {.notes}
StructuralIdentifiability.jl formalizes this result with differential
algebra. More data do not automatically help if they repeat the same
observation map; contact-pattern data or an externally measured c would.
:::

## API and validation

```julia
local_problem = ODEForwardSensitivityProblem(sir_kernel!, u0, (0.0, 40.0), p0)
local_solution = solve(local_problem, Tsit5(); saveat = tgrid)
states, jacobians = extract_local_sensitivities(local_solution, true)

identifiability = assess_identifiability(
    identifiability_system;
    measured_quantities = [y ~ b * c * S * I],
    funcs_to_check = [b, c, g, b * c],
)
```

- `SciMLSensitivity`: forward sensitivities or adjoints.
- `GlobalSensitivity`: Sobol first-order and total indices.
- `StructuralIdentifiability`: structural, noiseless identifiability.
- Check $S+I+R=N$ and compare one derivative with a finite difference.

::: {.notes}
The API snippet points to the full implementation in the book. The validation
checks numerical integrity, not historical adequacy or causal interpretation.
:::

## Takeaways and limitations

- Local: neighborhood behavior around one parameter vector.
- Global: ranking conditional on ranges and a design.
- Structural: information available in an idealized observation map.
- Practical identifiability also depends on noise, sampling, initial states, and misspecification.

Read the [book chapter](../../chapters/10-sensitivity-and-identifiability.html)
for derivations and exercises; see the
[SciMLSensitivity](https://docs.sciml.ai/SciMLSensitivity/stable/),
[GlobalSensitivity](https://docs.sciml.ai/GlobalSensitivity/stable/), and
[StructuralIdentifiability](https://docs.sciml.ai/StructuralIdentifiability/stable/)
documentation for APIs.

::: {.notes}
Close by asking which conclusion is about the model and which is about the
data. That question is the bridge to intervention analysis and the capstone.
:::
